Headteacher Message
Miss Harsha Patel
Welcome to our school website!
I am delighted to introduce you to our wonderful community of learners, teachers, and staff. Acton Gardens Primary School is a place where every child is valued and nurtured, every teacher is passionate and dedicated, and every member of staff is supportive and professional. We are committed to providing a high-quality education that prepares our students for the challenges and opportunities of the 21st century. We believe in developing the whole child — fostering their academic, social, and emotional growth.
Our school values of Aspiration, Growth, Perseverance, and Success underpin everything we do. We encourage every child to aim high, embrace learning, keep trying even when things are challenging, and celebrate their achievements, big and small.
Our children are wonderful ambassadors for our school, so if you would like to know more about our school family, please do get in touch. Our pupils and I would be delighted to show you around and introduce you to everyone who makes Acton Gardens such a special and incredible place to learn and grow.
Our school aim is Always striving for excellence, and our vision is Learning together for the future. We also believe in cultivating a culture of respect, responsibility, and kindness among our pupils, staff, and families.
This website is a window into our vibrant and dynamic learning environment. Here, you will find information about our curriculum, events, achievements, and much more.
I hope you enjoy exploring our website and discovering what makes Acton Gardens so unique. If you have any questions or feedback, please do not hesitate to contact us. We look forward to hearing from you and welcoming you to our Acton Gardens family.
Our Vision
Our school aims to provide a ambitious broad and balanced curriculum that develops the knowledge and skills pupils need to thrive now and for a fulfilling future. We believe that every pupil has the potential to grow and achieve excellence in their learning and personal development. We support our pupils to develop resilience and confidence in themselves and their capacity for growth.
We foster a culture of respect and inclusion, where pupils feel valued, value others and learn to work together to make a positive contribution in the community. We encourage creativity in an innovative learning environment, where pupils are challenged and inspired to explore their passions and talents.
We promote the wellbeing of our pupils, ensuring they stay safe and healthy in mind and body. We also help them appreciate the spiritual, moral, social and cultural richness of the world at large, and prepare them to become responsible global citizens.

pageCache.pageTitle: Special Educational Needs (SEN) Policy – Acton Gardens Primary School
pageCache.text:
Inclusion - Special Educational Needs and Disabilities
All children may experience some difficulties in learning from time to time during their school life. We aim to provide equal access to the whole curriculum for all children including those with special educational needs and/or disabilities (SEND). All teaching staff are involved in the learning and development of pupils with SEND. Parents and carers are involved at all stages
We place great emphasis on identifying pupils with additional needs as early as possible, therefore ensuring a differentiated curriculum to accommodate individual needs and allow maximum access to the curriculum. Where a child has a particular individual need, we will make reasonable adjustments to help them overcome their difficulties which may include additional support. Depending on the identified need this support may take place in class, in a small group or on an individual basis. On occasion, additional support is sought from an external agency such as, School Health, the Behaviour Support service, or the Educational Psychology Service
All Ealing Local Authority (LA) maintained schools have a similar approach to meeting the needs of pupils with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities and are supported by the LA to ensure that all pupils, regardless of their specific needs, make the best possible progress in school. All schools are supported to be as inclusive as possible, with the needs of pupils with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities being met in a mainstream setting wherever possible. The four broad ‘areas of need’ are Communication and Interaction, Cognition and Learning, Social, Emotional and Mental Health Difficulties, and Sensory and Physical Needs
Special Educational Needs and Disabilities Policy
Acton Gardens Primary School is committed to providing an inspiring, safe and caring environment in which all pupils are challenged and supported to maximise their potential
Our special educational needs and disability policy aims to:
This is based on the statutory Special Educational Needs and Disability (SEND) Code of Practice and the following legislation:
At our school we strive to create an inclusive teaching environment that offers all pupils, no matter their needs and abilities, a broad, balanced and challenging curriculum. We are committed to offering all pupils the chance to thrive and fulfil their aspirations
We will achieve this by making reasonable adjustments to teaching, the curriculum and the school environment to make sure that pupils with SEND are included in all aspects of school life
4.1 Special educational needs
A pupil has SEN if they have a learning difficulty or disability that requires special educational provision to be made for them.
They have a learning difficulty or disability if they have:
• A significantly greater difficulty in learning than most others of the same age, or• A disability which prevents or hinders them from making use of facilities of a kind generally provided for others of the same age in mainstream schools
Special educational provision is educational or training provision that is additional to, or different from, that made generally for other children or young people of the same age by mainstream schools.
Pupils are considered to have a disability if they have a physical or mental impairment that has a substantial and long-term adverse effect on their ability to do normal daily activities.
The school will make reasonable adjustments for pupils with disabilities, so that they are not at a substantial disadvantage compared with their peers.
The needs of pupils with SEND are grouped into 4 broad areas. Pupils can have needs that cut across more than 1 area, and their needs may change over time
Interventions will be selected that are appropriate for the pupil’s particular area(s) of need, at the relevant time
Communication and interaction• Pupils with needs in this area have difficulty communicating with others. They may have difficulty understanding what is being said to them, have trouble expressing themselves, or do not understand or use the social rules of communication.• Pupils who are on the autism spectrum often have needs that fall in this category.
Cognition and learningPupils with learning difficulties usually learn at a slower pace than their peers.
A wide range of needs are grouped in this area, including:
• Specific learning difficulties, which impact 1 or more specific aspects of learning, such as: dyslexia, dyscalculia and dyspraxia• Moderate learning difficulties• Severe learning difficulties• Profound and multiple learning difficulties, which is where pupils are likely to have severe and complex learning difficulties as well as a physical disability or sensory impairment
Social, emotional and mental healthThese needs may reflect a wide range of underlying difficulties or disorders. Pupils may have:
• Mental health difficulties such as anxiety, depression or an eating disorder• Attention deficit disorder, attention deficit hyperactive disorder or attachment disorder• Suffered adverse childhood experiences
These needs can manifest in many ways, for example as challenging, disruptive or disturbing behaviour, or by the pupil becoming withdrawn or isolated.
Sensory and/or physical Pupils with these needs have a disability that hinders them from accessing the educational facilities generally provided.
Pupils may have:• A sensory impairment such as vision impairment, hearing impairment or multi-sensory impairment• A physical impairment
These pupils may need ongoing additional support and equipment to access all the opportunities available to their peers.
5.1 The SENCOThe SENCO at Acton Gardens Primary School is Miss C Rose, who can be contacted at senco@agprimary.org.uk
She will:• Work with the headteacher and SEN governor to determine the strategic development of the SEND policy and provision in the school• Have day-to-day responsibility for the operation of this SEND policy and the coordination of specific provision made to support individual pupils with SEN, including those who have EHC plans• Provide professional guidance to colleagues and liaise and work with staff, parents, and other agencies to make sure that pupils with SEN receive appropriate support and high-quality teaching• Advise on the graduated approach to providing SEN support and differentiated teaching methods appropriate for individual pupils• Advise on the deployment of the school’s delegated budget and other resources to meet pupils’ needs effectively• Be a point of contact for external agencies, especially the local authority (LA) and its support services, and work with external agencies to ensure that appropriate provision is provided• Liaise with potential next providers of education to make sure that the pupil and their parents are informed about options and that a smooth transition is planned• When a pupil moves to a different school or institution: Make sure that all relevant information about a pupil’s SEN and the provision for them are sent to the appropriate authority, school or institution in a timely manner• Work with the headteacher and school governors to make sure the school meets its responsibilities under the Equality Act 2010 with regard to reasonable adjustments and access arrangements• Make sure the school keeps its records of all pupils with SEND up to date and accurate• With the headteacher, monitor to identify any staff who have specific training needs regarding SEN, and incorporate this into the school’s plan for continuous professional development• With the headteacher, regularly review and evaluate the breadth and impact of the SEND support the school offers or can access, and co-operate with the LA in reviewing the provision that is available locally and in developing the local offer• Prepare and review information for inclusion in the school’s SEN information report and any updates to this policy• With the headteacher and teaching staff, identify any patterns in the school’s identification of SEN, both within the school and in comparison with national data, and use these to reflect on and reinforce the quality of teaching
5.2 The SEND link governorThe SEND link governor is Mary Collier.The SEND governor will:
• Help to raise awareness of SEND issues at governing board meetings• Monitor the quality and effectiveness of SEND provision within the school and update the governing board on this• Work with the headteacher and SENCO to determine the strategic development of the SEND policy and provision in the school
5.3 The headteacherThe headteacher will:
• Work with the SENCO and SEND link governor to determine the strategic development of the SEND policy and provision within the school• Work with the SENCO and school governors to make sure the school meets its responsibilities under the Equality Act 2010 with regard to reasonable adjustments and access arrangements• Have overall responsibility for, and awareness of, the provision for pupils with SEND, and their progress• Have responsibility for monitoring the school’s notional SEND budget and any additional funding allocated by the LA to support individual pupils• Make sure that the SENCO has enough time to carry out their duties• Have an overview of the needs of the current cohort of pupils on the SEND register• Advise the LA when a pupil needs an EHC needs assessment, or when an EHC plan needs an early review• With the SENCO, monitor to identify any staff who have specific training needs regarding SEN, and incorporate this into the school’s plan for continuous professional development• With the SENCO, regularly review and evaluate the breadth and impact of the SEND support the school offers or can access, and co-operate with the LA in reviewing the provision that is available locally and in developing the local offer• With the SENCO and teaching staff, identify any patterns in the school’s identification of SEN, both within the school and in comparison with national data, and use these to reflect on and reinforce the quality of teaching
5.4 Class teachersEach class teacher is responsible for:
• Planning and providing high-quality teaching that is differentiated to meet pupil needs through a graduated approach• The progress and development of every pupil in their class• Working closely with any teaching assistants or specialist staff to plan and assess the impact of support and interventions, and consider how they can be linked to classroom teaching• Working with the SENCO to review each pupil’s progress and development, and decide on any changes to provision• Ensuring they follow this SEND policy and the SEN information report• Communicating with parents regularly to:• Set clear outcomes and review progress towards them > Discuss the activities and support that will help achieve the set outcomes > Identify the responsibilities of the parent, the pupil and the school > Listen to the parents’ concerns and agree their aspirations for the pupil
5.5 Parents or carersParents or carers should inform the school if they have any concerns about their child’s progress or development.
Parents or carers of a pupil on the SEND register will always be given the opportunity to provide information and express their views about the pupil’s SEND and the support provided. They will be invited to participate in discussions and decisions about this support. They will be:
• Invited to termly meetings to review the provision that is in place for their child• Asked to provide information about the impact of SEN support outside school and any changes in the pupil’s needs• Given the opportunity to share their concerns and, with school staff, agree their aspirations for the pupil• Given an annual report on the pupil’s progress
The school will take into account the views of the parent or carer in any decisions made about the pupil.
5.6 The pupilPupils will always be given the opportunity to provide information and express their views about their SEND and the support provided. They will be invited to participate in discussions and decisions about this support. This might involve the pupil:
• Explaining what their strengths and difficulties are• Contributing to setting targets or outcomes• Attending review meetings• Giving feedback on the effectiveness of interventions
The pupil’s views will be taken into account in making decisions that affect them, whenever

7.1 Identifying pupils with SEND and assessing their needs
The school has a clear approach to identifying and responding to SEND, and recognises that early identification and effective provision improves long-term outcomes for the pupils.
With the support of the SLT, classroom teachers will conduct regular progress assessments for all pupils, with the aim of identifying pupils who are making less than expected progress.
Class teachers will regularly assess the progress of all pupils and identify any whose progress:

PE Sports Premium Support
The Government is providing funding to schools to spend on improving the quality of sport and PE for all their children. The sport funding can only be spent on sport and PE provision in schools
Purpose of funding
Schools will have to spend the sport funding on improving their provision of PE and sport, but they will have the freedom to choose how they do this
Possible uses for the funding include: hiring specialist PE teachers or qualified sports coaches, paying for professional development opportunities for sport, running sport competitions and a sports council, or increasing participation in the school games, purchasing sports resources & equipment, providing places for pupils on after school sport clubs and holiday clubs

Wrap Around Care
Breakfast & After School Club (Aktiva)
At Acton Gardens Primary School, we are proud to offer affordable and flexible childcare to support our working families. Our breakfast and after-school clubs, run in partnership with Aktiva, take place in the safe and nurturing environment of our school, supervised by familiar and trusted school staff.
We have created a relaxed and welcoming atmosphere where children can play, create, engage and, most importantly, have fun.
Free Breakfast Club
Our free breakfast club is operated by Aktiva and gives children a calm and positive start to the day, with breakfast and time to socialise with friends before lessons begin.

Holiday Camps With Aktiva
Aktiva also runs multi-activity holiday camps at Acton Gardens Primary School during selected school holidays. The camps are open to children aged 4–11 from Acton Gardens Primary School and other schools.
Children can enjoy a varied programme of sports, games, arts, crafts and creative activities in a safe and welcoming school environment, supported by Aktiva’s trained and caring team.
The standard camp day runs from 9:00 am to 3:30 pm, with an extended day available until 5:00 pm.

Curriculum by Subject
Acton Gardens Primary School’s Art curriculum is built upon the CUSP (Curriculum with Unity Schools Partnership) scheme of learning, offering a well-rounded and progressive approach that nurtures creativity and artistic expression among pupils. The CUSP framework ensures a structured development of skills, allowing pupils to explore various artistic techniques, materials, and styles throughout their primary years.
In the Art curriculum, pupils engage with diverse media, including drawing, painting, sculpture, and digital art. Each unit encourages exploration and experimentation, allowing pupils to develop their unique artistic voice while learning about the work of renowned artists and art movements. This contextual understanding enriches their creative processes and fosters an appreciation for art in its many forms.
The CUSP scheme also emphasises the importance of critical thinking and reflection, enabling pupils to evaluate their own work and that of their peers constructively. Through collaborative projects and individual assignments, pupils learn to express their ideas and emotions visually, enhancing their communication skills.
By integrating art into the wider curriculum, Acton Gardens promotes cross-curricular connections that enrich learning experiences. Overall, the Art curriculum at Acton Gardens inspires pupils to think creatively, embrace challenges, and appreciate the role of art in culture and society.

Acton Gardens Primary School’s Design and Technology (D&T) curriculum, aligned with the CUSP (Curriculum with Unity Schools Partnership) scheme of learning, provides a structured and engaging approach to developing students’ practical and creative skills. CUSP’s framework emphasizes building foundational knowledge and skills progressively, allowing students to explore, create, and evaluate in a systematic and enjoyable manner.
The curriculum at Acton Gardens focuses on hands-on experiences where students actively engage with materials, tools, and design processes. Through the CUSP scheme, the school aims to foster innovation and problem-solving abilities in students, encouraging them to think critically about the world around them. Lessons are designed to inspire curiosity and creativity, covering key areas such as mechanisms, structures, textiles, food, and electronics. Each topic is broken down into specific objectives that align with the National Curriculum, ensuring that students are building skills that will be valuable in the future.
An important element of the CUSP approach is its emphasis on reflection and improvement, allowing students to evaluate their work and consider how their designs could be refined. Acton Gardens Primary School’s implementation of CUSP ensures a well-rounded D&T education, equipping students with skills for modern, tech-savvy, and innovative learning. Acton Gardens Primary School’s Geography curriculum is uniquely designed to reflect the vibrant community and local environment of the school, providing students with a highly relevant and engaging learning experience. Rather than using a generic program, the curriculum has been tailored to connect with the students’ surroundings and cultural backgrounds, allowing them to relate more personally to the material. This approach ensures that geographical concepts are not only taught but also lived and observed within their own community.
The curriculum covers core geographical skills and knowledge, such as map reading, understanding physical and human geography, and environmental awareness, but does so through a local lens. For example, students explore topics like urban development, green spaces, and sustainability in the context of their own neighborhood, learning how global issues affect their local environment. Field trips to nearby parks, rivers, and urban areas further enhance their learning by allowing students to see and experience geographical concepts firsthand.
By focusing on real-world issues and their impact on the local community, the Geography curriculum at Acton Gardens helps students appreciate the importance of place and their role within it. This context-driven approach encourages curiosity, environmental stewardship, and a stronger sense of connection to both their community and the wider world. Use the link below to see our progression map.
Acton Gardens Primary School’s History curriculum is designed with a tailored approach to reflect the unique context and diverse community of the school. Rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all program, the curriculum has been thoughtfully developed to include local history and themes that resonate with the backgrounds and experiences of our pupils. This approach not only meets National Curriculum requirements but also provides a more engaging, meaningful educational experience.
The curriculum encourages students to explore both British and global history, emphasizing stories and contributions from a wide array of cultures and perspectives. Local historical sites, events, and influential figures are woven into the curriculum, helping students develop a sense of connection to their surroundings and fostering pride in their community’s heritage. By integrating the local area’s rich history, students gain a deeper understanding of how historical events and figures have shaped the place they live.
Additionally, the curriculum focuses on developing key historical skills, such as critical thinking, analysis, and evidence evaluation. By learning through a context-specific lens, Acton Gardens’ pupils gain not only historical knowledge but also an appreciation for diversity and the impact of history on contemporary society, building well-rounded, culturally aware learners. Acton Gardens Primary School uses the Big Cat reading scheme as the foundation of its reading curriculum, aiming to instill a love of reading and a strong literacy foundation in its students. The Big Cat books are carefully leveled, offering a rich variety of fiction, nonfiction, and poetry that caters to diverse interests and reading abilities.
This approach ensures that every student is challenged appropriately, developing their decoding, comprehension, and critical thinking skills as they progress through the levels. Each year group also engages with a termly class reader, a carefully chosen book that provides a rich foundation for literacy development. This shared text becomes a central piece of the term’s literacy focus, guiding both reading comprehension and writing activities.
By immersing students in a captivating story or theme, the class reader inspires two major writing projects each term: a narrative piece and a non-narrative piece. For the narrative, students draw on the characters, setting, and plot elements they’ve explored in the class reader, learning to craft their own stories with creativity and depth. For the non-narrative piece, students might create reports, explanations, or persuasive texts that link to themes, ideas, or informational aspects found in the class reader. This dual approach not only reinforces understanding of the text but also helps students to apply their learning in varied writing contexts, developing both storytelling and factual writing skills in meaningful ways.
In grammar, Acton Gardens emphasizes key skills that are woven into both reading and writing lessons. Core skills like sentence structure, punctuation, and parts of speech are explicitly taught and practiced, giving students the tools to express their ideas clearly. By focusing on these grammar skills within meaningful contexts, the school ensures students develop as effective communicators.
Acton Gardens Primary School has adopted the White Rose Maths scheme as its main approach for teaching mathematics, a decision rooted in the program’s focus on mastery and progressive understanding of mathematical concepts. White Rose Maths is a widely respected scheme that aligns with the UK National Curriculum and emphasizes developing a deep, long-lasting understanding of maths in students from early years through to Key Stage 2.
By choosing White Rose, Acton Gardens Primary School aims to cultivate a strong mathematical foundation in its students, enabling them to approach problems with confidence and resilience. The scheme breaks down maths concepts into small, manageable steps, which allows students to explore topics in depth rather than merely covering content quickly. This methodology not only aids those who may struggle with mathematics but also challenges advanced learners through problem-solving tasks and reasoning activities that foster critical thinking.
Teachers at Acton Gardens benefit from White Rose’s extensive resources, including lesson plans, assessments, and engaging visuals, which support consistency across year groups. The school’s commitment to White Rose Maths reflects its dedication to high standards and ensuring that every student achieves a solid grasp of mathematical principles, preparing them well for their future education.
At Acton Gardens Primary School, the French curriculum for Key Stage 2 pupils (Years 3 to 6) is based on the Twinkl French Scheme, a comprehensive programme that encourages both linguistic and cultural learning. Through Twinkl’s engaging and well-structured resources, children are gradually introduced to the French language in a way that builds their confidence, vocabulary, and understanding over time.
Starting in Year 3, pupils focus on the basics of French, such as greetings, numbers, colours, and everyday phrases. Lessons incorporate interactive activities, songs, and games, making language learning enjoyable and accessible for young learners. As they progress into Years 4 and 5, children expand their vocabulary and begin constructing simple sentences about familiar topics like family, food, and hobbies. Twinkl’s scheme places an emphasis on spoken French, helping pupils practise pronunciation and conversational skills from an early stage.
By Year 6, students are exploring more complex aspects of the language, including reading short texts, writing simple sentences, and discussing topics related to French culture and traditions. This curriculum not only aims to build language proficiency but also fosters an appreciation for cultural diversity. Acton Gardens’ use of Twinkl ensures a supportive and progressive learning journey, enabling pupils to approach secondary language studies with enthusiasm and a strong foundation.

At Acton Gardens Primary School, the music curriculum is enriched by the Charanga Music Scheme, providing a structured, engaging approach to music education from Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) through to Year 6. The scheme is designed to foster musical development at each stage, offering a well-rounded experience that nurtures children’s enjoyment of music alongside their technical skills and musical understanding.
In EYFS, pupils begin by exploring sounds, rhythm, and movement, using playful activities to build confidence and introduce fundamental musical concepts. As they progress into Key Stage 1, they start to engage with singing, listening, and simple percussion instruments, focusing on timing, pitch, and expression. Lessons incorporate a range of musical genres, helping children appreciate diversity in music.
In Key Stage 2, pupils delve deeper into musical theory, reading basic notation, and exploring various instruments, including keyboards and recorders. The Charanga Scheme provides a strong foundation in both performance and composition, with interactive resources that support individual and group work. By Year 6, pupils are confident in performing, evaluating music critically, and creating their own compositions.
Through Charanga’s creative and child-centred approach, Acton Gardens ensures that every child experiences music as a dynamic, expressive form of learning, preparing them with skills that go beyond the classroom.

Acton Gardens Primary School’s Physical Education (PE) curriculum is enhanced by the PE Passport scheme of work, providing a comprehensive framework that promotes physical literacy, health, and well-being. This curriculum not only focuses on developing essential motor skills and fitness but also places a strong emphasis on competitive sports and external tournaments. Through partnerships with local schools and Featherstone High School, students are given numerous opportunities to participate in a variety of inter-school competitions, fostering teamwork and sportsmanship.
The curriculum is designed to cater to all students, encouraging them to engage in diverse physical activities, from traditional team sports to individual pursuits. Regular participation in competitions allows students to showcase their skills, build confidence, and experience the thrill of teamwork and rivalry.
Acton Gardens Primary School’s commitment to excellence in physical education is recognized by its attainment of the Platinum Award from the School Sports Partnership (SSP). This prestigious accolade reflects the school’s dedication to providing high-quality PE experiences and promoting an active lifestyle among its pupils. pageCache.pageTitle: Curriculum & Learning – Acton Gardens Primary School
pageCache.text:
Curriculum & Learning
Intent Statement
Acton Gardens Primary School is committed to meeting the requirements of the primary National Curriculum. Our schemes of work reflect the content and challenge of the curriculum. Teachers have received training in key areas of the curriculum and are ready to provide outstanding curriculum provision. The curriculum will be taught with consideration for the needs of all learners. Our ambitious curriculum has also been tailored to meet the needs of our children, and our local community. It will inspire children and nurture a passion for learning.
Implementation
We ensure that all children have access to an ambitious, broad, creative, balanced curriculum with Numeracy and Literacy at the heart of all learning. Skills and knowledge are taught in all subject areas; we ensure there is a progression of skills, across each subject, which is built upon each year and mapped across the key stages. The building blocks of our curriculum have been developed to allow children to learn more, remember more in a vocabulary rich enquiry based curriculum. We ensure that children have the opportunity to deepen their understanding by making links with reading and writing across all topics, which embeds transferable skills throughout. Trips and visits are a keystone of our learning to enthuse, immerse and deepen knowledge in our topics. The foundation subjects are taught through a half termly focus. This includes Geography, History, Art, Design Technology, Music, PE, Computing, RE, PSHE, and French (Y3 – 6).
Impact
We plan our lessons with clear learning objectives, which are based upon the teacher’s detailed knowledge of each child. Reflective teaching and ongoing summative assessment, leads to planning that is constantly adapted to the needs of the individual classes.
Children are expected to make good or better progress in all subjects and this individual progress is tracked termly. Pupils are assessed in reading, writing, maths and phonics at the end of each term. Subsequent year group progress meetings identify the needs of a year group to ensure that they are on track to make expected progress or that there are support plans in place. From these an action plan is created for the future term. SLT and subject leads use this in their monitoring of teaching and learning.

SEND and Inclusion
Our School Vision
Acton Gardens Primary School: Always striving for excellence and learning together for the future.
Our school aims to provide a broad and balanced curriculum that develops the knowledge and skills pupils need to thrive now and for a fulfilling future. We believe that every pupil has the potential to grow and achieve excellence in their learning and personal development. We support our pupils to develop resilience and confidence in themselves and their capacity for growth.
We foster a culture of respect and inclusion, where pupils feel valued, value others and learn to work together to make a positive contribution in the community. We encourage creativity in an innovative learning environment, where pupils are challenged and inspired to explore their passions and talents.
We promote the wellbeing of our pupils, ensuring they stay safe and healthy in mind and body. We also help them appreciate the spiritual, moral, social and cultural richness of the world at large, and prepare them to become responsible global citizens.

Our SENDCO is Mrs Charlotte Lee. She can be contacted on 020 8993 9053 or via senco@agprimary.org.uk.
